title: Heart
summary: The heart is a four-chambered muscular pump that moves about 5 liters of blood per minute.

layers.basics: Your heart is a fist-sized muscle that squeezes about 100,000 times a day to push blood around your body.
layers.deeper: It has two upper chambers (atria) and two lower chambers (ventricles). The right side sends blood to the lungs; the left side sends it to the rest of the body. Valves keep blood flowing one way.
layers.expert: A pacemaker region, the sinoatrial node, starts each beat. The impulse spreads across the atria, pauses at the AV node, then travels via the His-Purkinje system so the ventricles contract from the apex upward. Cardiac muscle is fed by the coronary arteries during diastole.

did_you_know: The heart starts beating about 3 weeks after conception, before most other organs exist.
open_questions: Can the adult human heart be induced to regenerate substantial muscle after injury?

title: Right atrium
summary: Upper right chamber that receives oxygen-poor blood from the body.

layers.basics: It collects blood returning from the body via the vena cava.
layers.deeper: Contains the SA node near the superior vena cava opening and pumps blood to the right ventricle.
layers.expert: Thin-walled; pectinate muscles; fossa ovalis is the remnant of the fetal foramen ovale; receives the coronary sinus.

facts: Upper right chamber that receives oxygen-poor blood from the body
did_you_know: The right atrium contains the heart's natural pacemaker.

title: Left atrium
summary: Upper left chamber that receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs.

layers.basics: Freshly oxygenated blood from the lungs arrives here.
layers.deeper: Four pulmonary veins drain into it; the left atrial appendage is a small pouch.
layers.expert: Located posteriorly; atrial fibrillation often arises from pulmonary vein ectopy and leads to clots in the appendage.

facts: Upper left chamber that receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs
did_you_know: The left atrium's appendage is where most atrial-fibrillation clots form.

title: Right ventricle
summary: Lower right chamber that pumps blood to the lungs.

layers.basics: This chamber pushes blood into the lungs, a short low-pressure trip.
layers.deeper: Its wall is thin relative to the left because pulmonary pressure is low.
layers.expert: Crescentic shape wrapped around the septum; peak systolic pressure ≈ 25 mmHg; moderator band carries conduction fibers.

facts: Lower right chamber that pumps blood to the lungs
did_you_know: Its output equals the left ventricle's beat for beat, though at lower pressure.

title: Left ventricle
summary: The strongest chamber: it pumps blood to the whole body.

layers.basics: The thick-walled chamber that sends blood out to the body at high pressure.
layers.deeper: Its muscle wall is about 1 cm thick and generates around 120 mmHg in systole.
layers.expert: Conical with helical fiber orientation producing twist; ejection fraction normally 55-70%; supplies coronary perfusion in diastole.

facts: The strongest chamber: it pumps blood to the whole body
did_you_know: The left ventricle alone makes the pulse you feel.

title: Interventricular septum
summary: The muscular wall separating the left and right ventricles.

layers.basics: This wall keeps oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood apart.
layers.deeper: It is mostly thick muscle with a small membranous part at the top.
layers.expert: Carries the bundle branches; ventricular septal defects are among the commonest congenital heart anomalies.

facts: The muscular wall separating the left and right ventricles
did_you_know: Both ventricles share this wall and push against each other slightly with each beat.

title: Tricuspid valve
summary: Valve between right atrium and right ventricle.

layers.basics: A one-way door with three flaps.
layers.deeper: Tied to the ventricle wall by thin cords so it does not flip backward.
layers.expert: Chordae tendineae and papillary muscles prevent prolapse; annulus ≈ 10-11 cm circumference.

facts: Valve between right atrium and right ventricle
did_you_know: Its name just means 'three points'.

title: Mitral valve
summary: Valve between left atrium and left ventricle.

layers.basics: A two-flap door named for its resemblance to a bishop's hat.
layers.deeper: It closes when the ventricle squeezes, producing part of the 'lub' sound.
layers.expert: Bicuspid with anterior and posterior leaflets; mitral regurgitation and stenosis are common valve diseases.

facts: Valve between left atrium and left ventricle
did_you_know: Named after a bishop's mitre.

title: Aortic valve
summary: Valve between left ventricle and aorta.

layers.basics: This three-cup valve opens as blood is pushed out to the body.
layers.deeper: Its cups fill and close the valve when the ventricle relaxes, making the 'dub' sound.
layers.expert: Sinuses of Valsalva give rise to the coronary arteries; aortic stenosis is common with aging.

facts: Valve between left ventricle and aorta
did_you_know: It opens and closes about 100,000 times a day.

title: Pulmonary valve
summary: Valve between right ventricle and pulmonary artery.

layers.basics: Another three-cup valve letting blood leave toward the lungs.
layers.deeper: Prevents backflow into the right ventricle.
layers.expert: A semilunar valve at the top of the right ventricular outflow tract, with three cusps that close under back-pressure.

facts: Valve between right ventricle and pulmonary artery
did_you_know: In the Ross procedure, a surgeon swaps a diseased aortic valve with the patient's own pulmonary valve.

title: Sinoatrial (SA) node
summary: The heart's natural pacemaker.

layers.basics: A cluster of special cells in the right atrium that sets the heartbeat rhythm.
layers.deeper: Its cells spontaneously fire about 60-100 times per minute.
layers.expert: Pacemaker cells use the funny current (If, HCN4) and calcium clock; autonomic input modulates rate.

did_you_know: Without an SA node signal, other cells take over at a slower pace.

title: Atrioventricular (AV) node
summary: A relay that delays the heartbeat signal before it reaches the ventricles.

layers.basics: The signal pauses here for a fraction of a second so the atria can finish emptying.
layers.deeper: It is the only normal electrical connection between atria and ventricles.
layers.expert: Slow conduction (≈ 0.05 m/s) from calcium-channel-based action potentials; secondary pacemaker (40-60 bpm).

facts: A relay that delays the heartbeat signal before it reaches the ventricles
did_you_know: The AV node holds the signal for about a tenth of a second.

title: Coronary arteries
summary: The arteries that feed the heart muscle itself.

layers.basics: The heart needs its own blood supply, delivered by arteries on its surface.
layers.deeper: Left and right coronary arteries start just above the aortic valve and branch around the heart.
layers.expert: Mostly filled in diastole; blockage by atherosclerosis causes angina and myocardial infarction. Coronary flow ≈ 250 mL/min at rest.

facts: The arteries that feed the heart muscle itself
did_you_know: The heart muscle receives most of its blood only while it is relaxed.

title: Aorta
summary: The body's largest artery, carrying oxygen-rich blood from the heart.

layers.basics: The aorta is the main highway for blood leaving the heart; all other arteries branch from it.
layers.deeper: Its elastic walls stretch with each beat and recoil to keep blood flowing smoothly between beats (Windkessel effect).
layers.expert: Segments: ascending, arch, descending thoracic, abdominal; diameter ≈ 2.5-3.5 cm; pulse wave velocity ≈ 4-10 m/s rises with stiffness.

did_you_know: The aorta's elastic recoil keeps blood moving between heartbeats.

title: Vena cava
summary: The two great veins that return oxygen-poor blood to the heart.

layers.basics: The superior vena cava drains the upper body; the inferior drains the lower.
layers.deeper: Veins have thin walls and low pressure; muscle pumps and valves help return blood.
layers.expert: IVC lacks valves except a rudimentary Eustachian valve; ≈ 2 cm diameter; venous return influenced by respiratory pump.

did_you_know: The inferior vena cava is the largest vein.

title: Carotid arteries
summary: Paired neck arteries that carry blood to the head and brain.

layers.basics: You can feel a pulse on either side of your neck from these arteries.
layers.deeper: Each splits into an internal branch (brain, eye) and an external branch (face, scalp).
layers.expert: The carotid sinus contains baroreceptors; carotid bodies sense O2/CO2; plaque here is a major stroke cause.

did_you_know: Pressing the carotid sinus can slow the heart rate.

title: Artery
summary: Thick-walled vessels carrying blood away from the heart.

layers.basics: Arteries are strong tubes with muscular walls that handle high pressure.
layers.deeper: They branch into smaller arterioles.
layers.expert: Three layers (intima, media, adventitia); elastic arteries (aorta) and muscular arteries; arterioles are the main site of resistance.

did_you_know: Arteries are named for the Greek for 'air pipes' since they were found empty after death.

title: Vein
summary: Thin-walled vessels returning blood to the heart.

layers.basics: Veins are wider and softer than arteries and have valves to stop blood falling backward.
layers.deeper: Squeezing leg muscles pushes blood up through them.
layers.expert: Hold ≈ 60-70% of blood volume (capacitance vessels); valves prevent backflow; varicose veins arise from valve failure.

did_you_know: Your veins hold most of your blood at any moment.

title: Capillary
summary: Microscopic vessels where blood swaps gases, nutrients and waste with tissues.

layers.basics: Capillaries are so thin that red blood cells squeeze through single file.
layers.deeper: Their walls are just one cell thick, so oxygen and nutrients can pass.
layers.expert: Continuous, fenestrated and sinusoidal types; exchange governed by Starling forces; ≈ 5-10 µm diameter.

did_you_know: Capillaries are so narrow that red blood cells deform to pass through.

title: Blood
summary: The fluid tissue that carries oxygen, nutrients, hormones, heat and immune cells.

layers.basics: Blood is about half liquid plasma and half cells. It carries almost everything your body needs and wastes it needs to get rid of.
layers.deeper: Red cells carry oxygen, white cells fight infection, platelets stop bleeding, and plasma carries proteins, salts, sugars and hormones.
layers.expert: Hematocrit ≈ 40-45%; plasma ≈ 55%, of which water ≈ 92%; albumin ≈ 4 g/dL; pH 7.35-7.45.

did_you_know: A drop of blood holds about 5 million red cells.

title: Nose, nasal cavity and pharynx
summary: The upper airway that warms, moistens and filters air.

layers.basics: Air enters through the nose, where hairs and mucus trap dust, and warms up on its way to the lungs.
layers.deeper: The nasal cavity has a rich blood supply and mucus-coated lining with cilia.
layers.expert: Turbinates create turbulent flow to humidify air to ≈ 100% relative humidity at body temperature; olfactory epithelium sits at the roof.

did_you_know: Your nose alternates which nostril is dominant every few hours.

title: Larynx
summary: The voice box that guards the airway and produces sound.

layers.basics: The larynx holds your vocal cords. They vibrate when air passes to make your voice.
layers.deeper: Cartilages and muscles move the vocal folds, and the epiglottis closes the airway when you swallow.
layers.expert: Phonation by Bernoulli effects and mucosal wave; fundamental frequency ≈ 100-120 Hz (typically lower voices) to ≈ 200-250 Hz; superior and recurrent laryngeal nerves.

did_you_know: Your voice pitch is set by vocal-fold length and tension, not by 'size of the throat'.

title: Trachea (windpipe)
summary: A flexible tube reinforced by C-shaped cartilage rings that carries air to the lungs.

layers.basics: The windpipe leads from the throat to the lungs and is kept open by rings of cartilage.
layers.deeper: Its inner lining of ciliated cells sweeps mucus and trapped dust upward (mucociliary escalator).
layers.expert: 16-20 C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings; posterior trachealis muscle permits esophageal expansion; bifurcates at the carina near T4-T5.

did_you_know: Cilia in your airways beat about 10-15 times each second.

title: Left lung
summary: The left lung exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide with the blood. It has two lobes.

layers.basics: Lungs are spongy, air-filled organs. When you breathe in, oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.
layers.deeper: Airways branch about 23 times from the trachea down to the alveoli. The left lung has a notch (cardiac notch) for the heart.
layers.expert: Lungs are surrounded by a double-layered pleura and held against the chest wall by negative pleural pressure (≈ -5 cmH2O at rest). Surfactant lowers surface tension, and dual blood supply comes from pulmonary and bronchial circulations.

did_you_know: Lung tissue is so light that it would float on water.

title: Right lung
summary: The right lung exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide with the blood. It has three lobes.

layers.basics: Lungs are spongy, air-filled organs. When you breathe in, oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.
layers.deeper: Airways branch about 23 times from the trachea down to the alveoli. The right lung is slightly larger and has three lobes.
layers.expert: Lungs are surrounded by a double-layered pleura and held against the chest wall by negative pleural pressure (≈ -5 cmH2O at rest). Surfactant lowers surface tension, and dual blood supply comes from pulmonary and bronchial circulations.

did_you_know: Lung tissue is so light that it would float on water.

title: Bronchi
summary: Large airways branching from the trachea into each lung.

layers.basics: Two main tubes split off the windpipe and fork into smaller and smaller branches.
layers.deeper: Cartilage plates keep them open.
layers.expert: Primary, lobar and segmental bronchi; lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells.

did_you_know: The right main bronchus is wider and straighter, so inhaled objects more often end up there.

title: Bronchioles
summary: Small airways without cartilage that regulate airflow.

layers.basics: Tiny airway twigs that tighten or relax to control airflow.
layers.deeper: Smooth muscle tone adjusts diameter; asthma narrows them.
layers.expert: Terminal and respiratory bronchioles (< 1 mm); site of small-airway resistance; Club cells secrete protective proteins.

did_you_know: They have no cartilage, only muscle, so they can clamp down in an asthma attack.

title: Alveoli
summary: Microscopic air sacs where gases pass into and out of the blood.

layers.basics: Each lung has hundreds of millions of tiny sacs wrapped in capillaries.
layers.deeper: Their walls are one cell thick so oxygen can diffuse across in a fraction of a second.
layers.expert: ≈ 480 million alveoli total, diameter ≈ 200 µm; type I cells for exchange, type II cells make surfactant; blood-gas barrier ≈ 0.2-0.6 µm.

did_you_know: The alveolar surface is often compared to a tennis court, but measured values (~50-100 m²) are closer to a studio apartment.

title: Diaphragm
summary: The dome-shaped muscle under the lungs that powers breathing.

layers.basics: When you breathe in, the diaphragm flattens and pulls air into the lungs.
layers.deeper: It separates chest from abdomen. Hiccups are spasms of this muscle.
layers.expert: Innervated by the phrenic nerves (C3-C5); contributes ≈ 60-70% of quiet inspiratory volume; excursion ≈ 1.5 cm quiet, up to 10 cm deep.

did_you_know: The phrenic nerve starts in the neck, far above the diaphragm, because the muscle migrates down during development.
